content.text:
6.1 Algebra Play
Over the last two years, we have used algebra to model different situations. We have learned how to solve algebraic equations and find the values of unknown letter-numbers. Let's now have some fun with algebra. We shall investigate tricks and puzzles, and explain why they work using algebra. We will also see how to invent new tricks and puzzles to entertain others.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a friend says, think of any number, add 3, double it, take away 6, and halve it. Can the friend say what you will get without asking your number?
2. Try it with 4 and with 10. Each time you get back the number you started with.
3. Is it luck with the numbers we picked, or must it always happen? Keep this question open: by the end of the chapter letter-numbers will answer it, and you will build tricks of your own.

media.tool_name: Trick Builder: Make the Letter Cancel

tool_config.idea: A Think of a Number trick ends on a fixed value when the starting number cancels. Changing a number in one step changes the final value, and a step that does not cancel the start breaks the trick.
tool_config.title: Trick Builder: Make the Letter Cancel
tool_config.screen: A cup holding the starting number x, a row of step cards (double, add, multiply, divide, add or subtract the start) with editable numbers, and a trace of the expression after each step next to the value for a chosen start.
feedback: A trick whose x does not cancel shows two different endings for two starts, side by side.
When x cancels the trace shows a plain number and the trick is marked as always working.
A built trick is checked by running it on three starting numbers.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with each trick checked on more than one start.

media.instructions_for_student: A Think of a Number trick ends on a fixed value when the starting number cancels. Changing a number in one step changes the final value, and a step that does not cancel the start breaks the trick.
media.description:
The student opens a small magic stage. On the left is a cup holding the secret starting number x. Beside it is a row of step cards: double it, add a number, halve it, multiply, divide, or subtract the start. Every card has an editable number. The student drags cards into a row to build a Think of a Number trick, types the numbers on the cards, then picks a starting number and presses Run. The value appears after every step.

First the student runs the same trick on two or three different starts and sees whether the endings match. Then the student switches on the trace, which writes what is happening to x after every step. They watch x appear, get doubled, get halved, and in the best tricks vanish at the last step. The student changes one number on a card and sees the final value change, which shows that the number added or taken away decides the ending. A trick whose x does not cancel shows two different endings for two starts, side by side. A trick where x cancels shows a plain number in the trace and is marked as always working.

The six cards ask the student to make a trick end on 3 and then on 5 by choosing one number, to find the final value of tricks that multiply and divide, to test whether a trick that ends by adding the start still works, and finally to invent their own trick of at least four steps that always ends on 7, checked on two starts. Hints move from asking what is left after the halving step, to writing each step with x, to showing that halving 2x plus a number leaves x plus half the number. Through doing, the student learns that a trick is not magic: the letter cancels, and the cancelling is what makes the answer the same for every start.

tool_config.idea: In the date trick every answer is 100M + 165 + D. Taking 165 away leaves the month followed by a two digit day, so the date can be read straight back from the answer.
tool_config.title: Date Trick Decoder: Reading the Hidden Date

A month that is too large or a day past 31 is flagged on the split.
A correct date is confirmed by running the steps forward to the reported answer.

media.instructions_for_student: In the date trick every answer is 100M + 165 + D. Taking 165 away leaves the month followed by a two digit day, so the date can be read straight back from the answer.
media.description:
The student sits at a decoder desk with a month and day picker on one side and the six steps of the date trick laid out one after another, each showing its running value. Below sit an answer box and a Subtract box that splits what is left into a month part and a day part.

In the first part the student picks a month and a day, runs the six steps, and reads the answer. For month 3 and day 14 they see how the answer is built from the month and day. In the second part the roles swap. A reported answer is typed in, the student subtracts 165, and then splits what is left. The last two digits are the day and the digits before them are the month. The split view shows the digits in two coloured groups so the student can see where each part is hiding.

Every decoded date is checked by running the steps forward and comparing with the reported answer. If the date is wrong, the answer that comes out is shown beside the reported one so the student can see the gap. A month that is too large or a day past 31 is flagged on the split. The cards include answers like 874, 1167 and 1396, one where the day has a zero in front and the student must say why, and one such as 500 that no real date can give. A step editor lets the student change the trick, for example multiply the month by 20, add 3, multiply by 5, add the day, and then find the new number to subtract. Hints ask where the month and day are hiding, then suggest taking away the fixed number the steps add, then name 165. The student learns that every answer has the form 100 times the month, plus 165, plus the day, which is why the date can always be read back.

content.text:
6.2 Thinking about 'Think of a Number' Tricks
In Grade 7, we learned about 'Think of a Number' tricks, like this one.
1. Think of a number. 2. Double it. 3. Add four. 4. Divide by two. 5. Subtract the original number you thought of.
I predict you get 2. Am I right? Try it out with different starting numbers. Do you always end up with the same value, 2? Why?
We saw that we can understand such tricks through algebra.
1. Think of a number: x. 2. Double it: 2x. 3. Add four: 2x + 4. 4. Divide by 2: x + 2. 5. Subtract the original number you thought of: x + 2 − x = 2.
Therefore, no matter what the starting number is, the end result will always be 2!

content.text:
1. Predict first: will the trick give 2 for a large number like 50 as well as for 5?
2. Try 5 and 11. Both end on 2.
3. Now call the number x. Doubling gives 2x, adding four gives 2x + 4, halving gives x + 2, and taking away x leaves 2.
4. The x cancels out, so the start does not matter. Trying a few numbers shows a pattern; the letter shows it must always hold.

Worked example: Try the trick (double, add four, divide by two, subtract the start) with 5 and with 11, then explain with a letter-number why it always ends on 2.
1. Start with 5: 5 × 2 = 10, then 10 + 4 = 14, then 14 ÷ 2 = 7, then 7 − 5 = 2.
2. Start with 11: 11 × 2 = 22, then 22 + 4 = 26, then 26 ÷ 2 = 13, then 13 − 11 = 2.
3. Start with x: double it to get 2x, add four to get 2x + 4, divide by 2 to get x + 2.
4. Subtract the start: x + 2 − x leaves 2, whatever x is.
Answer: It always ends on 2, because the starting number cancels out

content.text:
Let us now look at a different trick of this type.
Shubham: Think of a date. Multiply the month by 5. Add 6. Multiply by 4. Add 9. Multiply by 5. Add the day. Tell me your answer.
Mukta thinks of 26 January and reports 291. Shubham says: You thought of our Republic Day.
How did Shubham figure out the date chosen by Mukta?
Let the month be M and the day be D. Multiply M by 5: 5M. Add 6: 5M + 6. Multiply by 4: 20M + 24. Add 9: 20M + 33. Multiply by 5: 100M + 165. Add the day: 100M + 165 + D.
Mukta's answer was 291. 291 = 100M + 165 + D. 291 − 165 = 100M + D. 126 = 100M + D.
Since D is a day within a month, it is atmost 31 and requires only 2 digits. So the last 2 digits are D and what comes before that is M. In this case, M is 1 and D is 26, i.e., the 26th of January.

content.text:
Think of a Number tricks: find the dates: Find the dates if the final answers of the date trick are the following: (i) 1269 (ii) 394 (iii) 296.
1. (i) 1269 − 165 = 1104: the day is 04 and the month is 11, so 4 November.
2. (ii) 394 − 165 = 229: the day is 29 and the month is 2, so 29 February, a leap year date.
3. (iii) 296 − 165 = 131: the day is 31 and the month is 1, so 31 January.
Answer: (i) 4 November (ii) 29 February (iii) 31 January

media.instructions_for_student: Each box of a number pyramid is the sum of the two boxes below it. Going up we add, going down we subtract, and with letters in the bottom row the top of a three row pyramid is a + 2b + c.
media.description:
The student sees a number pyramid of three or four rows made of boxes. The bottom boxes accept numbers or letters. Any box can be locked as a given, and a Letters switch changes every box into an expression in the bottom row.

Going up, the student types a bottom row such as 2, 7, 5 and watches each row above fill in, every box being the sum of the two below it. Before pressing reveal, the student predicts the top, and a wrong guess shows how many times each bottom box was counted. Going down, the student locks the top and a few other boxes and fills the rest by subtracting. A box filled by adding is marked, and the subtraction that should have been used is shown. With a top of 40 and a bottom row of 10, a blank and 6, the student puts a letter in the blank and solves for it.

With Letters on, a three row pyramid shows the top as a + 2b + c, so the student sees that the middle bottom box feeds both middle boxes and is counted twice. In the four row pyramid with all ones at the bottom, the student predicts the top from a + 3b + 3c + d and checks it. The last card builds a pyramid on 2, 3, 5, 8 and asks whether every box is a Virahanka-Fibonacci number. Hints ask which boxes the top depends on, then suggest counting the paths from each bottom box to the top. A letter answer is checked by putting the value back and rebuilding the pyramid. The student learns that the top of a pyramid can be found without building it, and that going down is an equation with one unknown.

narration: <bookmark mark='names'/>Step one, call the middle blocks eigh and bee, and the bottom blank see.
<bookmark mark='eqs'/>The rule gives three equations.
Eigh plus bee is sixty, twelve plus see is eigh, and see plus eight is bee.

beats.on_screen: middle row a and b, bottom blank c: a + b = 60; 12 + c = a; c + 8 = b

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step two, put twelve plus see for eigh, and see plus eight for bee.
<bookmark mark='join'/>That gives twenty plus two see equals sixty.
Both middle blocks use see, so the top equation has only see left.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Step three, take away twenty from sixty to get two see equals forty.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Divide by two, and see is twenty.
We undo the adding first and then the doubling, so we take away and then divide.
<bookmark mark='a'/>Step four, eigh is twelve plus twenty, which is thirty two.
<bookmark mark='b'/>Bee is twenty plus eight, which is twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check, thirty two plus twenty eight is sixty.
Now see is known, so the middle blocks follow by adding.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The middle row is thirty two and twenty eight, and the bottom row is twelve, twenty and eight.

6.3 Number Pyramids
In a number pyramid, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly below it (see the figure).
Bottom row 1, 9, 4; middle row 10, 13; top 23.
Use the same rule to fill these pyramids: bottom row 6, 2; bottom row 3, 4, 3; bottom row 5, 4, 5, 0.

content.text:
Worked example: Fill the pyramids with bottom rows 6, 2 and 3, 4, 3 and 5, 4, 5, 0.
1. Bottom row 6, 2: the top is 6 + 2 = 8.
2. Bottom row 3, 4, 3: the middle row is 3 + 4 = 7 and 4 + 3 = 7, and the top is 7 + 7 = 14.
3. Bottom row 5, 4, 5, 0: the next row is 5 + 4 = 9, 4 + 5 = 9 and 5 + 0 = 5.
4. Then 9 + 9 = 18 and 9 + 5 = 14, and the top is 18 + 14 = 32.
Answer: Tops 8, 14 and 32

content.text:
Worked example: A pyramid has top 10, middle row 4 and a blank, and bottom row 1 and two blanks. Fill it.
1. The middle blank is 10 − 4 = 6.
2. Below the 4 sit 1 and a blank, so that blank is 4 − 1 = 3.
3. Below the 6 sit 3 and the last blank, so it is 6 − 3 = 3.
4. Check going up: 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 3 = 6, 4 + 6 = 10.
Answer: Middle row 4, 6; bottom row 1, 3, 3

content.text:
What about filling in the numbers in this pyramid? Where do we start? Top 60; middle row two blanks; bottom row 12, a blank, 8.
Let us fill the empty boxes with letter-numbers. From the rules for filling up pyramids, we get the following equations. a + b = 60. 12 + c = a. c + 8 = b.
From this, we see that, (12 + c) + (c + 8) = a + b = 60. Hence, 20 + 2c = 60. 2c = 60 − 20 = 40. c = 20.
Once we know c, we can find a and b, and complete the pyramid.

Answer: Middle row 32, 28; bottom row 12, 20, 8

content.text:
Worked example: Fill the four row pyramid with top 50, second row a blank and 22, and bottom row 4, a blank, 6, a blank.
1. Call the bottom blanks p and q: the bottom row is 4, p, 6, q.
2. Third row: 4 + p, p + 6, 6 + q. The 22 is (p + 6) + (6 + q), so p + q + 12 = 22 and p + q = 10.
3. The top is (4 + p) + 2(p + 6) + (6 + q), which is 3p + q + 22, so 3p + q + 22 = 50 and 3p + q = 28.
4. Take p + q = 10 away from 3p + q = 28: that leaves 2p = 18, so p is 9 and q is 1.
5. Third row 13, 15, 7; second row 28, 22; check 28 + 22 = 50.
Answer: Bottom row 4, 9, 6, 1; third row 13, 15, 7; second row 28, 22

Worked example: Fill the pyramid with second row 40 and a blank, third row ending in 9, and bottom row 5, a blank, 7, a blank. Then fill the pyramid with top 35, third row ending in 7, and bottom row 3, 5, two blanks.
1. Second pyramid: the last bottom box is 9 − 7 = 2. Call the other blank p.
2. The 40 is (5 + p) + (p + 7), so 2p + 12 = 40 and p is 14. Third row 19, 21, 9; second row 40, 30; top 40 + 30 = 70.
3. Third pyramid: call the bottom blanks r and s, so r + s = 7 from the 7 above them.
4. The top is 3 + 3 × 5 + 3r + s, so 18 + 3r + s = 35 and 3r + s = 17. With r + s = 7, 2r = 10, so r is 5 and s is 2.
5. Third row 8, 10, 7; second row 18, 17; check 18 + 17 = 35.
Answer: First: bottom 5, 14, 7, 2 and top 70. Second: bottom 3, 5, 5, 2 with rows 8, 10, 7 and 18, 17

content.text:
Worked example: Write the top of a three row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c. Use it for the bottom row 1, 9, 4.
1. The middle row is a + b and b + c.
2. The top is (a + b) + (b + c), which is a + 2b + c.
3. For 1, 9, 4: 1 + 2 × 9 + 4 = 23.
4. Building it gives 10, 13 and then 23, the same top.
Answer: The top is a + 2b + c; for 1, 9, 4 it is 23

Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 2): Write an expression for the topmost row of a pyramid with 4 rows in terms of the values in the bottom row.
1. Bottom row a, b, c, d. The next row is a + b, b + c, c + d.
2. The row above that is a + 2b + c and b + 2c + d.
3. The top is (a + 2b + c) + (b + 2c + d), which is a + 3b + 3c + d.
Answer: a + 3b + 3c + d

The top is (a + 2b + c) + (b + 2c + d), which is a + 3b + 3c + d.

3. 7, 18, 19, 6: 7 + 54 + 57 + 6 = 124.
4. 9, 7, 5, 11: 9 + 21 + 15 + 11 = 56.

content.text:
Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 4): Recall the Virahanka-Fibonacci number sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, ... where each number is the sum of the two numbers before it. If the first three Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a number pyramid with three rows, fill in the rest of the pyramid. What numbers appear in the grid? What is the number at the top? Are they all Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers?
1. The bottom row is 1, 2, 3.
2. The middle row is 1 + 2 = 3 and 2 + 3 = 5.
3. The top is 3 + 5 = 8.
4. The sequence goes 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so every number in the grid is in it.
Answer: The grid holds 1, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 8; the top is 8; all are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers

Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 5): What can you say about the numbers in the pyramid and the number at the top in the following cases? (i) The first four Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a four row pyramid. (ii) The first 29 Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a 29 row pyramid.
1. (i) Bottom row 1, 2, 3, 5. Next row 3, 5, 8. Next row 8, 13. Top 8 + 13 = 21.
2. All of them are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, and the top 21 is the 7th number of 1, 2, 3, 5, ...
3. Two neighbours in the sequence add to the number two places further on, so every row is again a run of Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, moved two places along.
4. (ii) Each row moves two places along, so after 28 steps up the single top box is the 57th number of the sequence.

Answer: (i) All are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers and the top is 21 (ii) All are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers and the top is the 57th number of the sequence

content.text:
Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 6): If the bottom row of an n row pyramid contains the first n Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, what can we say about the numbers in the pyramid? What can we say about the number at the top?
1. Two neighbours of the sequence add to the number two places further on.
2. So each row is a run of Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, starting two places further along than the row below.
3. The bottom row starts at the 1st number, so the top row, n − 1 steps up, is the number at place 1 + 2(n − 1), which is the (2n − 1)th number.
4. Check: n = 3 gives the 5th number, 8; n = 4 gives the 7th number, 21.
Answer: Every number in the pyramid is a Virahanka-Fibonacci number, and the top is the (2n − 1)th number of the sequence

media.instructions_for_student: In an algebra grid every shape is a fixed number and each row shows a sum. A row with one kind of shape gives it at once; otherwise rows can be added or taken apart to free one shape at a time.
media.description:
The student is shown an algebra grid. Each row is made of shapes and ends in a sum. Beside every shape type is a value box. A row turns green when the values typed in make its sum true, and stays red otherwise.

The student first reads all the rows and decides which to solve first. A row with one kind of shape, such as three triangles making 21, gives that shape at once. When a shape is typed into a value box, every row where it appears updates, so the student sees one value shared across the whole grid. This corrects the idea that two squares in different places could be different numbers.

When no row is easy, the student can add two rows. The combined row shows how many times each shape now appears, so rows like two squares with a circle making 23 and two circles with a square making 22 can be joined and divided to free a shape. A row with a wrong sum stays red and the shapes it uses are marked, and a shape value is confirmed only when every row it appears in is true. The six cards move from a single-row start, to two shapes in two rows, to one where the answer of an earlier card is reused to fill the sum of a new row, and end with a grid where the student must also check that the two shapes have different values. Hints ask which row is easiest first, then suggest adding rows so each shape appears the same number of times, then name the division step. The student learns to write each row as an equation, combine rows to remove one unknown, and check an answer in every row.

media.instructions_for_student: In a calendar block, the date to the right is one more and the date below is seven more. So every block can be written in terms of its top left date, and its sum gives that date away.
media.description:
The student opens a month calendar with a movable frame. The frame can be a 2 by 2 square, a column of three, a 3 by 3 square or an L shape. The dates inside it can be shown as numbers or as expressions in a, where a is the top left date, together with the sum and its expression.

The student drags the frame across the calendar and watches the sum change while the expression in a stays the same. Looking at a 2 by 2 block, they see that the date to the right is a + 1, the date below is a + 7 and the one diagonal is a + 8, so the sum is 4a + 16. Then the dates are hidden. The student reads only the sum, writes it as an equation in a, and finds the block, for example the four dates for a sum of 64, or the middle date of a 3 by 3 frame with sum 117.

Each answer is checked by placing the frame on the block that was found. A wrong block highlights the date that breaks the plus 1 or plus 7 pattern, and a sum that cannot be made, such as a block running past the end of the month, is flagged. The student also designs a new shape, writes its sum in terms of a and tests it on the calendar, and in the last card changes the calendar to ten columns and sees how the 2 by 2 sum changes. Hints ask what lies directly below any date, then suggest writing every date in terms of a, then show taking 16 away and dividing by 4. The student learns that one expression describes every block of a given shape, and that the sum gives the position away.

topics.summary: In a calendar block the dates are a, a + 1, a + 7 and a + 8, so their sum 4a + 16 gives a away. In an algebra grid each shape is an unknown number found from the row sums.

content.text:
6.4 Fun with Grids
Calendar Magic
A page from a calendar is given below. Your friend picks a 2 × 2 grid from this calendar, adds the 4 numbers in this grid and tells you the sum.
August 2025 block 6, 7, 13, 14: 6 + 7 + 13 + 14 = 40.
Can we find the 4 numbers in the grid from just knowing this sum?
Let us use algebra. Consider a 2 × 2 grid. Let a represent the top left number. What are the other numbers in terms of a? a, a + 1, a + 7, a + 8.
Adding all four numbers, the sum is a + (a + 1) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 4a + 16.
Suppose you are told that the sum is 36. Can you find the 4 numbers in the grid?
4a + 16 = 36. 4a = 20 (subtracting 16 from both sides). a = 5 (dividing both sides by 4).
Now that we have found a, we know that the other three numbers are a + 1, a + 7 and a + 8. Therefore, the grid must be the following: 5, 6, 12, 13.

content.text:
Worked example: In a grid, three squares make 27 and two circles with a square make 19. Find the square and the circle.
1. Three equal squares make 27, so one square is 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
2. Two circles and a square make 19, so two circles make 19 − 9 = 10.
3. One circle is 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
4. Check: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 and 5 + 5 + 9 = 19.
Answer: Square 9, circle 5

media.instructions_for_student: With three different digits, the largest two digit by one digit product uses the largest digit as the multiplier and the other two digits, in decreasing order, as the two digit number.
media.description:
The student sees three digit tiles and a product frame made of two boxes, a times sign and one box. Next to the frame is a table that records every arrangement tried, with its product, grouped by the multiplier.

The student drags the three digits into the frame and reads the product. For digits such as 2, 4 and 6 there are six arrangements, and the student tries them all, watching the table fill. The table pairs the arrangements that share a multiplier and marks the larger product in each pair, so the student can see that with the same multiplier, putting the larger digit in the tens place wins. The student then compares across multipliers, for example 93 times 6 against 63 times 9, and finds that the largest digit works best as the multiplier.

Before the table is complete, the student predicts the arrangement that gives the largest product. A wrong prediction shows the two products side by side with their place value parts, so the student can see which one gained more in the tens. After all six, the largest is highlighted and the rule is written out: largest digit as multiplier, other two in decreasing order. The cards cover 2, 4, 6, then 1, 5, 8, then 3, 6, 9, ask for the smallest product with 2, 7, 9, ask the student to predict first for 4, 5, 6, and finally let them choose three digits and test the rule. Hints ask which box changes the product most, then suggest comparing two arrangements with the same multiplier. The student learns why the rule works, not just what it is.

content.text:
6.5 The Largest Product
Fill the digits 2, 3, and 5 in a two digit number times a one digit number, using each digit once. What is the largest product possible?
Let us approach this problem systematically. There are six ways to place three digits: We can fill the first box with 2, 3 or 5. For each of these choices, we have 2 ways of filling the remaining 2 digits. The six options are 23 × 5, 25 × 3, 32 × 5, 35 × 2, 52 × 3, 53 × 2.
How do we find the largest product among these six options?
We can group them in pairs where the multiplier is the same. 35 × 2 and 53 × 2. 25 × 3 and 52 × 3. 23 × 5 and 32 × 5.
In each pair, the one with the larger multiplicand generates the larger product, so we can reduce the comparison to these three expressions. 53 × 2. 52 × 3. 32 × 5.
It is clear that 52 × 3 is bigger than 53 × 2, so we only need to compare 52 × 3 and 32 × 5. Let us expand these. 32 × 5 = (3 × 10 × 5) + (2 × 5). 52 × 3 = (5 × 10 × 3) + (2 × 3).
The first terms in both expressions are the same. The second term shows that 32 × 5 is larger, and hence the largest of the six possible products we can form with 2, 3 and 5.

Worked example: Place the digits 2, 3 and 5 to make the largest two digit by one digit product.
1. The six options are 23 × 5, 25 × 3, 32 × 5, 35 × 2, 52 × 3 and 53 × 2.
2. In each pair with the same multiplier keep the larger: 53 × 2, 52 × 3 and 32 × 5.
3. 53 × 2 = 106, 52 × 3 = 156 and 32 × 5 = 160.
4. By place value: 32 × 5 = 150 + 10 and 52 × 3 = 150 + 6, so 32 × 5 wins.
Answer: 32 × 5 = 160 is the largest product

content.text:
In this case, we used the largest digit as the multiplier. The other two digits were arranged in decreasing order to form the multiplicand. Will this always be the case? Let us find out using algebra.
Suppose p, q, and r are the three digits such that p < q < r.
As before, we have six possible products, which we group by the multiplier: qr × p, rq × p; pr × q, rp × q; pq × r, qp × r.
In each pair, the multiplicand with the larger tens digit forms the larger product. So we have three products to compare: rq × p, rp × q, qp × r.
Since q > p, we can see that rp × q is bigger than rq × p. This leaves us with a comparison between qp × r and rp × q. If we expand these, we get qp × r = (10 × q × r) + (p × r), rp × q = (10 × r × q) + (p × q).
Once again, the first term is the same in both expressions. Since r > q the second term of the first expression is larger, so the largest product is qp × r. This matches our earlier observation that the largest digit should be the multiplier and the other two digits should be arranged in decreasing order to form the multiplicand.

content.text:
Worked example: Show that qp × r is the largest product for digits p < q < r, and check it with the digits 4, 6 and 8.
1. Keep the larger of each pair: rq × p, rp × q and qp × r.
2. Expand: rp × q is 10 × r × q plus p × q, and rq × p is 10 × r × p plus q × p. The ones parts match and q > p, so rp × q is bigger.
3. Expand: qp × r is 10 × q × r plus p × r, and rp × q is 10 × r × q plus p × q.
4. The tens parts match and p × r is bigger than p × q, so qp × r is the largest.
5. Check with 4, 6, 8: 64 × 8 = 512 and 84 × 6 = 504, so 64 × 8 wins.
Answer: qp × r is always the largest; for 4, 6 and 8 it is 64 × 8 = 512

media.instructions_for_student: Written in place value, a number and its reverse, cycles or repeats combine into a number with a hidden factor: reverse and subtract gives 9 times (b − a), reverse and add gives 11 times (a + b), cycling three digits and adding gives 111 times the digit sum, and repeating three digits multiplies by 1001.
media.description:
The student works in a digit lab with tiles for a two or three digit number, labelled with place values. An operation chooser offers four moves: reverse and subtract, reverse and add, cycle the digits and add, and repeat the digits. Under the chooser are the result and a divide by box.

The student picks digits and an operation, for example 52 reversed and subtracted, and reads the result. Then they try dividing it by a chosen number, such as 9, and see whether it leaves no remainder, and compare the quotient with the digit difference. A divisor that leaves a remainder is shown with the remainder and the place value view of the result. With the place value view switched on, the result is written as a fixed number times a digit expression: reverse and subtract gives 9 times the difference of the digits, reverse and add gives 11 times their sum, adding the two cycles of a three digit number gives 111 times the digit sum, so 37 divides it, and repeating three digits multiplies the number by 1001, which is why 7, 11 and 13 all divide it.

The six cards use 52, 74, 247, 163 and 841, and ask the student to test which of 9 and 11 always divides a number plus its reverse, trying 38 and 61. A correct divisor is confirmed by showing the number times a digit expression. Hints ask which operation is done to the number and its reverse, then suggest writing the number with place values and combining like parts. The student learns that a trick that seems to work for every number works because the letters combine into a fixed factor.

content.text:
6.6 Decoding Divisibility Tricks
It is now Mukta's turn to show a mathematics trick to Shubham.
Mukta: Choose a 2 digit number of different digits and don't reveal it! Reverse the digits to get another number. Find their difference. Divide the result by 9. There won't be any remainder.
Shubham thinks of 47, reverses it to 74, finds 74 − 47 = 27, and 27 ÷ 9 = 3. Shubham: Yes, you are right. But how did you know?
If we choose other 2 digit numbers, and follow the steps, will there always be no remainder?
Let's try to understand how Mukta's trick works. Suppose the two digit number is ab. When it is reversed, the new number is ba.
If b > a, then ba > ab. So, the difference is (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 10b − b − 10a + a = 9b − 9a = 9 (b − a).
The difference is divisible by 9.

Worked example: Take 352, reverse it to 253 and subtract. Show with letters why 99 always divides the difference of a three digit number and its reverse.
1. 352 − 253 = 99, and 99 ÷ 99 = 1.
2. Write abc as 100a + 10b + c and its reverse as 100c + 10b + a, with a larger than c.
3. The difference is 100a + c − 100c − a, the tens cancel, which is 99a − 99c.
4. That is 99 times (a − c), so 99 always divides it. For 352, the difference of the outer digits is 3 − 2 = 1.
Answer: The difference is 99 times the difference of the first and last digits

Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 2): In the trick given above, instead of finding the difference of the two 2 digit numbers, find their sum. What will happen? For example: 31 + 13 = 44, 28 + 82 = 110, 12 + 21 = 33. Observe that all these numbers are divisible by 11. Is this always true? Can we justify this claim using algebra?

2. The sum is 11a + 11b, which is 11 times (a + b).
3. So the sum is always divisible by 11, and the quotient is the digit sum: 44 ÷ 11 = 4 and 3 + 1 = 4.
Answer: Yes, always: the sum is 11 times the sum of the digits

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 3): Consider any 3 digit number, say abc (100a + 10b + c). Make two other 3 digit numbers from these digits by cycling these digits around, yielding bca and cab. Now add the three numbers. Using algebra, justify that the sum is always divisible by 37. Will it also always be divisible by 3? (Hint: Look at some multiples of 37.)
1. abc is 100a + 10b + c, bca is 100b + 10c + a and cab is 100c + 10a + b.
2. Each digit appears once as hundreds, once as tens and once as ones, so the sum is 111a + 111b + 111c.
3. That is 111 times (a + b + c), and 111 = 3 × 37.
4. Check with 123: 123 + 231 + 312 = 666, and 666 ÷ 37 = 18, 666 ÷ 3 = 222.
Answer: The sum is 111 times (a + b + c); since 111 = 3 × 37 it is always divisible by 37 and by 3

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 4): Consider any 3 digit number, say abc. Make it a 6 digit number by repeating the digits, that is abcabc. Divide this number by 7, then by 11, and finally by 13. What do you get? Try this with other numbers. Figure out why it works. (Hint: Multiply 7, 11 and 13.)
1. Try 254: 254254 ÷ 7 = 36322, then 36322 ÷ 11 = 3302, then 3302 ÷ 13 = 254.
2. Repeating the digits means abc × 1000 + abc, which is abc × 1001.
3. And 7 × 11 × 13 = 1001, so dividing by 7, 11 and 13 divides by 1001.
Answer: You get back the original 3 digit number, because abcabc is abc × 1001 and 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13

media.title: Rounds Machine: Double and Give

tool_config.idea: Each round doubles what is held and then gives some away, so the amount after n rounds is a letter expression in the start. Setting that expression equal to what is left finds the start, and the amount grows only while less is given than is held.
tool_config.title: Rounds Machine: Double and Give
tool_config.screen: A start box, a round panel with a double step and a give step, a number of rounds, and a trace of the amount after each round both as a number and as an expression in x.
feedback: A wrong prediction runs the rounds one at a time and shows where the amounts differ.
A start that reaches the target is checked by running every round forward.
The x view shows how each round doubles the expression before the give step takes away.

hint_ladder.text: What happens to the amount in one round, in order?
Follow x through the first round, then the second, and set the last expression equal to what is left.

The start is filled in and the rounds are run forward to check it; a new card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: Each round doubles what is held and then gives some away, so the amount after n rounds is a letter expression in the start. Setting that expression equal to what is left finds the start, and the amount grows only while less is given than is held.
media.description:
The student sees a start box, a round panel with a double step and a give step, a counter for the number of rounds, and a trace that shows the amount after each round as a number and as an expression in x.

First the student predicts. If the amount doubles in each round but some is given away, does it always grow? They set a start, an amount to give and a number of rounds, for example 6 coins, give 5, two rounds, write a guess, and press Run. The trace shows the amount after each round. A wrong prediction runs the rounds one at a time and shows where the amounts differ. With start 8 and give 8 in every round, the student sees that the amount never grows, and works out why: it grows only while less is given than is held.

Next the student switches to the x view. Each round doubles the whole expression before the give step takes some away. For double and give 5 for two rounds, the amount is written in terms of x, and setting it equal to what is left becomes an equation. In the reverse task, the student sets a target and searches for the start that reaches it, such as double and give 3 for two rounds ending with 11, or give 4 for three rounds ending with 20. A start that reaches the target is checked by running every round forward. Hints ask what happens in a round and in what order, then suggest following x through the first round, then the second. The student learns to follow a story step by step, in order, and to turn it into an equation.

media.title: Swap Counter: Heads and Legs

tool_config.idea: When every item is of the lighter kind the total is too small. Swapping one item for the heavier kind adds the same difference each time, so the number of swaps is the shortfall divided by that difference.
tool_config.title: Swap Counter: Heads and Legs
tool_config.screen: A row of counters for the total heads, a table of two kinds with their legs, wheels or rupees, and a running total. Each tap swaps one counter to the other kind and the total changes. A letter view writes the equation.
feedback: A total that cannot be reached by whole swaps is flagged with the amount left over.
Each swap shows the difference it adds, so the same step can be seen every time.
A solution is checked by counting the heads and the total again.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with each answer checked against the heads and the total.

hint_ladder.text: What would the total be if every counter were of the lighter kind?
Find how far that total is from the target and how much one swap adds.
Divide the shortfall by what one swap adds to get the number of swaps.
The swaps are made and both kinds are counted; a new card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: When every item is of the lighter kind the total is too small. Swapping one item for the heavier kind adds the same difference each time, so the number of swaps is the shortfall divided by that difference.
media.description:
The student sees a row of counters for the total number of heads, a small table of two kinds with their legs, wheels or rupees, and a running total. Each tap swaps one counter from the lighter kind to the heavier kind and the total changes. A letter view writes the equation.

The student starts with every counter of the lighter kind, for example 12 hens with 2 legs each, and reads the total, which is too small for 34 legs. Then they swap counters one at a time and watch the total climb. Each swap shows the difference it adds, here 2 legs, so the student can see the same step happening every time. They stop when the total matches the target and read off how many were swapped, which is the number of horses. A total that cannot be reached with whole swaps is flagged with the amount left over, which handles the case of 10 heads and 25 legs.

The cards move through 12 heads and 34 legs, 30 heads and 84 legs, 15 cycles with 38 wheels where bicycles have 2 and tricycles have 3, and 20 coins worth 70 rupees using 2 rupee and 5 rupee coins. In the last card the student lets h be the number of horses, writes the equation from the letter view and solves it. A solution is checked by counting the heads and the total again. Hints ask what the total would be if every counter were the lighter kind, then suggest finding the shortfall and how much one swap adds, then dividing. The student learns that the swapping method and the equation are the same idea: the shortfall divided by what one swap adds.

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step two, count the wheels.

content.text:
Worked example: A stand has 20 cycles, some bicycles and some tricycles, with 46 wheels in all. How many of each?
1. Let t be the number of tricycles, so there are 20 − t bicycles.
2. Wheels: 3t + 2(20 − t) = 46, so t + 40 = 46 and t is 6.
3. There are 6 tricycles and 14 bicycles. Check: 3 × 6 + 2 × 14 = 18 + 28 = 46.
4. Without letters: 20 bicycles would have 40 wheels; each tricycle adds 1 more, and 46 − 40 = 6.
Answer: 6 tricycles and 14 bicycles

content.text:
Worked example: Asha has some stickers. She doubles them and gives away 5, then doubles again and gives away 5. She has 13 left. How many did she start with?
1. Let x be the start. After round one she has 2x − 5.
2. After round two she has 2(2x − 5) − 5, which is 4x − 15.
3. So 4x − 15 = 13, which gives 4x = 28 and x is 7.
4. Check: 7 × 2 = 14, then 14 − 5 = 9, then 9 × 2 = 18, then 18 − 5 = 13.
Answer: She started with 7 stickers

content.text:
Worked example: A lemonade stall pays rent of ₹200 a day, and each glass costs ₹5 to make. If 60 glasses are sold, what price per glass gives a profit of ₹400?
1. Let the price be p rupees. Income is 60p.
2. Costs: rent 200 and making 60 × 5 = 300.
3. Profit: 60p − 300 − 200 = 400, so 60p = 900 and p is 15.
4. Check: 60 × 15 = 900, and 900 − 300 − 200 = 400.
Answer: ₹15 per glass

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 5): There are 3 shrines, each with a magical pond in the front. If anyone dips flowers into these magical ponds, the number of flowers doubles. A person has some flowers. He dips them all in the first pond and then places some flowers in shrine 1. Next, he dips the remaining flowers in the second pond and places some flowers in shrine 2. Finally, he dips the remaining flowers in the third pond and then places them all in shrine 3. If he placed an equal number of flowers in each shrine, how many flowers did he start with? How many flowers did he place in each shrine?
1. Let x be the start and k the flowers placed in each shrine.
2. After the first pond and shrine: 2x − k. After the second: 2(2x − k) − k, which is 4x − 3k.
3. The third pond doubles it to 8x − 6k, and all of it goes into shrine 3, so 8x − 6k = k and 8x = 7k.
4. The smallest whole numbers are x = 7 and k = 8. Check: 14 − 8 = 6, then 12 − 8 = 4, then 8.
5. Any multiple also works, such as 14 flowers with 16 in each shrine.
Answer: He started with 7 flowers and placed 8 in each shrine (or any multiple, like 14 and 16)

3. The third pond doubles it to 8x − 6k, and all of it goes into shrine 3, so 8x − 6k = k and 8x = 7k.
4. The smallest whole numbers are x = 7 and k = 8. Check: 14 − 8 = 6, then 12 − 8 = 4, then 8.
5. Any multiple also works, such as 14 flowers with 16 in each shrine.
Answer: He started with 7 flowers and placed 8 in each shrine (or any multiple, like 14 and 16)

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
A farm has some horses and hens.
<bookmark mark='counts'/>The total number of heads of these animals is fifty five,
and the total number of legs is one hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many horses and how many hens are on the farm?
Can you solve this without letter numbers?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a farm with horses and hens, 55 heads and 150 legs Photo: A village farm yard with a stable and a hen coop

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='heads'/>Every animal has one head, so there are fifty five animals.
<bookmark mark='legs'/>A horse has four legs, and a hen has two.
beats.on_screen: every animal has 1 head; a horse has 4 legs; a hen has 2 legs Photo: A horse standing in a field

marks.given: the numbers 55 heads and 150 legs are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, fifty five heads and one hundred fifty legs, from horses and hens.
beats.on_screen: Given: 55 heads; 150 legs; horses have 4 legs, hens have 2

marks.find: the aim is written on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many horses and how many hens there are.
beats.on_screen: To find: the number of horses and the number of hens

marks.let: h is written as the number of horses
marks.hens: 55 − h is written as the number of hens

narration: <bookmark mark='let'/>Step one, let aitch be the number of horses.
<bookmark mark='hens'/>There are fifty five animals, so the hens are fifty five take away aitch.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: let h = the number of horses; hens = 55 − h Photo: A horse in a field

marks.hens: 2 (55 − h) is written for the hen legs
marks.total: = 150 is written to finish the equation
marks.horses: 4h is written for the horse legs

beats.colours: horse legs and hen legs in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='horses'/>Step two, count the legs.
Each horse has four legs, so the horses have four aitch legs.
<bookmark mark='hens'/>Each hen has two legs, so the hens have two times, fifty five take away aitch.
<bookmark mark='total'/>All the legs add up to one hundred fifty.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: 4h + 2 (55 − h) = 150 Photo: A hen in a yard

narration: <bookmark mark='open'/>Step three, open the bracket.
Two times fifty five is one hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Four aitch take away two aitch is two aitch.
Then two aitch plus one hundred ten is one hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='aitch'/>Take away one hundred ten, and two aitch is forty.
Aitch is twenty.
We combine like terms, so only aitch is left on one side.

marks.hens: 55 × 2 = 110 is written for an all hen farm
marks.extra: 150 − 110 = 40 is written as the extra legs

narration: <bookmark mark='hens'/>Step four, try it without letters.
If all fifty five animals were hens, there would be one hundred ten legs.
<bookmark mark='extra'/>The real count is forty legs more.
Each horse in place of a hen adds two legs.
<bookmark mark='horses'/>Forty divided by two gives twenty horses, the same as before.
Each swap adds two legs, so the extra legs tell us the horses.
beats.on_screen: Step 4, without letters: 55 hens would have 55 × 2 = 110 legs; 150 − 110 = 40 extra; each horse adds 2; 40 ÷ 2 = 20

narration: <bookmark mark='hens'/>Step five, find the hens and check.
Fifty five take away twenty is thirty five hens.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Four times twenty is eighty, and two times thirty five is seventy.
Together that is one hundred fifty legs.
The legs must come to one hundred fifty, so the check proves it.

marks.ans: the answer 20 horses and 35 hens is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>There are twenty horses and thirty five hens.
beats.on_screen: Answer: 20 horses and 35 hens

video_script.design: One idea: a letter for the horses gives the hens as fifty five take away that letter, and the legs give the equation. The farm stays on the board and the check is the last step.
source: Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 6)

without letters: 55 hens have 110 legs; 150 − 110 = 40 extra; each horse adds 2; 40 ÷ 2 = 20
video_script.payoff_line: There are twenty horses and thirty five hens

final_answer.spoken: twenty horses and thirty five hens

video_script.substitution: Let h be the horses, hens 55 − h, legs 4h + 2 (55 − h) = 150; then 55 hens would have 110 legs, 40 extra, 40 ÷ 2 = 20 horses.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: let a letter be the horses, write the hens as fifty five take away that letter, and count the legs. Watch for students who forget that a hen has two legs and a horse has four.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
A mother is five times her daughter's age.

<bookmark mark='ask'/>How old is the daughter now?

marks.given: the two facts are written

beats.on_screen: Given: mother = 5 times the daughter now; in 6 years, mother = 3 times the daughter

beats.on_screen: To find: the daughter's age now

narration: <bookmark mark='let'/>Step one, let dee be the daughter's age now.
<bookmark mark='mum'/>The mother is five times as old, so she is five dee.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: let d = the daughter's age now; mother = 5d

marks.mum: 5d + 6 is written for the mother in 6 years
marks.girl: d + 6 is written for the daughter in 6 years

beats.colours: mother and daughter in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='mum'/>Step two, look six years ahead.
The mother will be five dee plus six.
<bookmark mark='girl'/>The daughter will be dee plus six.
<bookmark mark='eq'/>The mother is then three times the daughter.
That gives five dee plus six, equal to three times, dee plus six.
In six years both ages go up by six, so we add six to each.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: in 6 years, mother = 5d + 6, daughter = d + 6; 5d + 6 = 3 (d + 6)

marks.take: 3d is taken from both sides to give 2d + 6 = 18

narration: <bookmark mark='open'/>Step three, open the bracket.
Three times dee is three dee, and three times six is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Take three dee from both sides, and two dee plus six is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='dee'/>Take six from both sides, and two dee is twelve.
Dee is six.
We keep both sides balanced, so we do the same to both.
<bookmark mark='now'/>Step four, check with six.
The mother is five times six, which is thirty now.
<bookmark mark='later'/>In six years, she is thirty six and the daughter is twelve.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three times twelve is thirty six, as the question says.
The ages fit the question, so six is right.
beats.on_screen: Step 4, check: mother now 5 × 6 = 30; in 6 years 36 and 12; 36 = 3 × 12

marks.ans: the answer The daughter is 6 years old is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The daughter is six years old, and the mother is thirty.
beats.on_screen: Answer: The daughter is 6 years old

media.description: A dosa cart pays rent of five thousand rupees a day, and each dosa costs ten rupees to make. A letter for the price gives eighty rupees for one hundred dosas, and a letter for the number sold gives one hundred seventy five dosas at fifty rupees.

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 6): A farm has some horses and hens. The total number of heads of these animals is 55 and the total number of legs is 150. How many horses and how many hens are on the farm? Can you solve this without letter-numbers? (Hint: If all the 55 animals were hens, then how many legs would there be? Using the difference between this number and 150, can you find the number of horses?)
1. Let h be the horses, so there are 55 − h hens.
2. Legs: 4h + 2(55 − h) = 150, so 2h + 110 = 150 and h is 20.
3. Without letters: 55 hens would have 110 legs. 150 − 110 = 40 legs are extra, and each horse adds 2, so 40 ÷ 2 = 20 horses.
4. Hens: 55 − 20 = 35. Check: 4 × 20 + 2 × 35 = 80 + 70 = 150.
Answer: 20 horses and 35 hens
steps: Let h be the horses, so there are 55 − h hens.
Without letters: 55 hens would have 110 legs. 150 − 110 = 40 legs are extra, and each horse adds 2, so 40 ÷ 2 = 20 horses.

Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 7): A mother is 5 times her daughter's age. In 6 years' time, the mother will be 3 times her daughter's age. How old is the daughter now?
1. Let the daughter be d years old, so the mother is 5d.
2. In 6 years: 5d + 6 = 3(d + 6), which is 3d + 18.
3. So 2d = 12 and d is 6.
4. Check: the mother is 30 now; in 6 years 36 = 3 × 12.
Answer: The daughter is 6 years old

Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 8): Two friends, Gauri and Naina, are cowherds. One day, they pass each other on the road with their cows. Gauri says to Naina, "You have twice as many cows as I do". Naina says, "That's true, but if I gave you three of my cows, we would each have the same number of cows". How many cows do Gauri and Naina have?
1. Let Gauri have g cows, so Naina has 2g.
2. If Naina gives 3: 2g − 3 = g + 3, so g is 6.
3. Naina has 12. Check: 12 − 3 = 9 and 6 + 3 = 9.
Answer: Gauri has 6 cows and Naina has 12

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 9): I run a small dosa cart and my expenses are as follows: rent for the dosa cart is ₹5000 per day; the cost of making one dosa (including all the ingredients and fuel) is ₹10. (i) If I can sell 100 dosas a day, what should be the selling price of my dosa to make a profit of ₹2000? (ii) If my customers are willing to pay only ₹50 for a dosa, how many dosas should I aim to sell in a day to make a profit of ₹2000?
1. (i) Let the price be p. Income 100p; costs 5000 + 100 × 10 = 6000.
2. 100p − 6000 = 2000, so 100p = 8000 and p is 80.
3. (ii) Let n dosas be sold. Each earns 50 − 10 = 40 after its own cost.
4. 40n − 5000 = 2000, so 40n = 7000 and n is 175. Check: 175 × 40 = 7000.
Answer: (i) ₹80 per dosa (ii) 175 dosas a day

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 10): Evaluate the following sequence of fractions: 1 ÷ 3, (1 + 3) ÷ (5 + 7), (1 + 3 + 5) ÷ (7 + 9 + 11). What do you observe? Can you explain why this happens? (Hint: Recall what you know about the sum of the first n odd numbers.)
1. (1 + 3) ÷ (5 + 7) = 4 ÷ 12, which is one third.
2. (1 + 3 + 5) ÷ (7 + 9 + 11) = 9 ÷ 27, which is one third again.
3. The first n odd numbers add up to n × n, and the first 2n odd numbers add up to 4 × n × n.
4. So the next n odd numbers add up to 4 × n × n minus n × n, which is 3 × n × n, three times the top.
Answer: Every fraction equals one third, because the bottom sum is always three times the top sum

content.text:
Figure it Out (divisibility tricks, question 11): Karim and the Genie. Each time Karim goes around the banyan tree, the coins in his pocket double, and then he gives the genie 8 coins. After the third round the coins doubled, and he was left with only 8 coins, exactly the number he owed the genie. (i) How many coins did Karim initially have? (ii) For what cost per round should Karim agree to the deal, if he wants to increase the number of coins he has? (iii) Through its magical powers, the genie knows the number of coins that Karim has. How should the genie set the cost per round so that it gets all of Karim's coins?
1. (i) Let x be the start. After one round 2x − 8, after two rounds 4x − 24.
2. The third doubling gives 8x − 48, which is 8, so 8x = 56 and x is 7.
3. Check: 7, then 14 − 8 = 6, then 12 − 8 = 4, then 8, all given to the genie.
4. (ii) With cost c, one round turns x into 2x − c, which is more than x only when c is less than x. So Karim should agree only if the cost is less than the coins he starts with, here fewer than 7.
5. (iii) After three rounds he has 8x − 7c. For this to be 0, the genie sets c to 8x ÷ 7. For 7 coins that is 8 per round, exactly the genie's trick.
Answer: (i) 7 coins (ii) a cost per round less than his coins, fewer than 7 (iii) 8 ÷ 7 of his starting coins per round, which is 8 when he starts with 7

content.text:
Algebra is very useful in modeling and understanding numerical scenarios. Because of this, it occurs in almost all areas of mathematics, science and beyond.
Algebra is an indispensable tool in justifying mathematical statements.
We applied algebra to analyse 'Think of a Number' tricks, number pyramids, grids, ways of forming numbers using given digits to maximise certain products, divisibility tricks, and various other problems.

1. Our opening question is settled: the add 3, double, take away 6, halve trick always gives your number back, because with x it becomes x + 3, then 2x + 6, then 2x, then x.
2. A letter-number turns a pattern seen in a few cases into a statement true for every case.
3. Still open for you: invent a trick, a pyramid or a puzzle and use a letter to show why it works.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a set of games: tricks, pyramids, grids, products and puzzles. Each game is played with numbers first, the pattern is guessed, and then a letter-number explains why the pattern must hold. Students end each idea by inventing a trick or puzzle of their own.

points.text: Every trick is tried with two or three starting numbers before any letter appears, so the letter explains a pattern the student has already seen.
points.title: Play first, then explain

points.text: Nine tools, each used once: building a trick, decoding a date trick, a pyramid builder, a shape grid, a calendar frame, a digit arranger, a digit lab for 9, 11, 37 and 1001, a rounds machine, and a swap counter. The remaining tricks and puzzles are taught without a tool because the algebra itself is the move.
points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea

points.text: Every answer found with a letter-number is put back into the story or the grid to check it.
points.title: Check by substituting

points.text: Math Talk prompts ask for new tricks, new calendar shapes and new puzzles, built from the same algebra.
points.title: Invent your own
